design_detail: Narrative review (The Lancet, 'Review' article; 9 pages, 96 references, two panels and two UNODC maps) of the adverse health effects of non-medical cannabis use, by two Australian researchers (School of Population Health, University of Queensland; National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales). The Acknowledgments describe it as the updated version of a review first funded by the Australian Commonwealth Department of Health and Ageing in 1994 (updated in 2001 and 2003), linked to a report undertaken for the Beckley Foundation. A 'Search strategy and selection criteria' box names two databases, 14 search terms (editors' count) and a 10-year window; there are no inclusion criteria, record counts, appraisal of individual studies or pooling. Four causal criteria are stated (an association in case–control and prospective studies; reverse causation implausible; confounding controlled in prospective studies; biological plausibility). Topics: acute effects (toxicity, psychological effects, driving), pregnancy, dependence and withdrawal, respiratory effects, cancers, cardiovascular effects, cognition and brain imaging, education, other illicit drug use, psychosis, depression, suicide and potency. Panel 1 lists the effects the authors regard as probable; Panel 2 lists possible effects whose causal relation is unknown.
can_establish: How two Australian addiction researchers read the evidence on the adverse effects of regular cannabis use in 2009: which effects they judged probable or only possible, the causal criteria they applied, and which primary studies and figures they cited for each effect (useful as a map to the primary literature).
cannot_establish: Any effect size as first-hand evidence: every figure is second-hand, several reach the review through the authors' own 2003 book or other reviews, and some cannot be traced to a named primary study. Nor can it show that the evidence cited is complete (study selection is not explicit), that any association is causal (the authors call the common-cause explanation of the psychosis association difficult to exclude and leave the cognitive question unresolved), or anything about sleep (beyond insomnia listed as a withdrawal symptom), edibles, vaping or cannabinoid hyperemesis, which it does not discuss.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence came from a described search of PubMed and Thomson Reuters Web of Science for articles on adverse health effects published in the previous 10 years, plus publications found from those selected and from books, edited works and reports (Search strategy and selection criteria box, p. 1383).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No study-level criteria. Topic criterion only: the effects of greatest potential public-health interest, meaning those most likely to occur and to affect a substantial proportion of people who use cannabis (Summary, p. 1383; Health effects of cannabis, p. 1384). Most selected studies were in English and published since 1997.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cited studies come mainly from the USA, Australia, New Zealand and western Europe, with lung-cancer case–control data from the Maghreb.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. The single most-cited source is the authors' own book (Hall & Pacula, 2003, ref 5: 18 citations in the editors' count from the text extraction; the next most cited, Iversen's book, has 9). It carries pattern-of-use figures, the causal criteria, the treatment-outcome figure, the potency statements and several general claims. Five of 96 references have one of the review's authors as an author (refs 2, 5, 68, 77, 88) and two more are chapters in a book Hall co-edited (refs 18, 48). Several key figures come from books and chapters rather than from the database search (Iversen, 2008; Solowij, 1998; Anthony, 2006). The review covers harms only, by design.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level; the cited studies mostly used self-reported use, and the driving studies measured THC in blood or serum. The review states that there are no reliable data on the THC and cannabidiol content of commonly used products (p. 1383) and no data on THC dose in epidemiological studies (p. 1386).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Definitions used by the review: heavy or regular use is daily or almost daily use (p. 1383); chronic use is almost daily use over a period of years (p. 1386). The cited estimates use other exposures, which claims must carry with each figure: cannabis tried by age 18, and ten or more uses by 18 (Swedish conscripts); ever use, and the category the review calls regular use (pooled psychosis odds ratios); frequency of use at 16 (depression, suicide attempts); meeting criteria for cannabis dependence or abuse (suicide case–control study); blood THC above a threshold (driving); use before 17 (twin study of other drugs) and before 15 (school leaving); five or more joints a day for 10 or more years (one imaging study). Route: smoking is assumed throughout; no other route is discussed. Potency: US THC content given as under 2% in 1980, 4.5% in 1997 and 8.5% in 2006 (p. 1384).
exposure.polysubstance: The review states that cannabis use is highly correlated with use of alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drugs, all of which affect health, and that some epidemiologists doubt that statistical adjustment removes this confounding (Macleod et al., 2004) (p. 1386). Tobacco is named as the confounder for respiratory cancers, and alcohol, tobacco and other drugs for outcomes in children of mothers who used cannabis in pregnancy (pp. 1387, 1389). Alcohol is addressed for driving only in the Laumon et al. (2005) analysis, where a dose–response persisted after control for blood alcohol (p. 1385).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: For cognition, as cited: partial recovery after 2 years of abstinence (Solowij, 1998), persistent dose-related impairment after 28 days (Bolla et al., 2002) and recovery after 28 days (Pope et al., 2001); imaging after 26 hours (Block et al., 2000) and after 28 days of abstinence (Block et al., 2002) (p. 1387). No abstinence period is given for the other cognitive findings.

comparison.controls: Not applicable at review level. Comparators in the cited estimates: men who had not tried cannabis by 18 (Swedish conscripts); people who had not used cannabis (pooled psychosis estimates); people who had stopped using cannabis and people who never used it (injury admissions); non-culpable drivers and age- and sex-matched hospital controls (driving); community controls (cancers, suicide attempts); co-twins who had not used cannabis (other illicit drugs).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that people who use cannabis regularly differ from others before they start, in ways that could affect behavioural outcomes (p. 1386), that poor cognitive functioning is a risk factor for regular use (p. 1387), and that no psychosis study had assessed all major confounders (p. 1388). Genetic factors are named only as an uncontrolled confounder of outcomes in children exposed before birth (p. 1386); shared genetic liability to psychosis and cannabis use is not discussed.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (no data). Outcomes as the review names them: schizophrenia diagnosis (Swedish conscripts); psychotic symptoms or psychotic disorders (pooled estimates); depressive disorder; serious suicide attempts and self-harm; cannabis dependence (criteria and instrument not named); crash injury, crash culpability and fatal crashes attributable to cannabis; birthweight, birth defects and child development scores; bronchitis symptoms, lung function and emphysema; lung and head and neck cancers; myocardial infarction and mortality after infarction; cognitive tests (not named), event-related potentials, cerebral blood flow and brain volumes; early school leaving; later use of other illicit drugs; disease burden.
outcomes.operationalization: An effect counts as probable when, in the authors' judgment, the four causal criteria are met; effects are sorted into probable (Panel 1) and possible with unknown causal relation (Panel 2) (pp. 1384, 1388). No grading scale beyond this two-way split is defined.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed by the review; all are cited (sources in the key findings). Psychosis: 2.4 times (cannabis tried by 18) and 2.3 times (ten or more uses by 18) for a schizophrenia diagnosis over 15 years in Swedish conscripts; pooled OR 1.4 (95% CI 1.20–1.65) for ever use and 2.09 (1.54–2.84) for the regular-use category (psychotic symptoms or disorders). Depression: pooled OR 1.49 (1.15–1.94). Suicide attempts: adjusted OR 2 in one case–control study. Dependence: lifetime risk about 9% among people who use cannabis and one in six when use starts in adolescence; 32% for nicotine, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine, 15% alcohol and 11% stimulants. Driving: RR 1.96 (injury admissions, men); OR 2.5 and 6.6 (culpability); OR 2.87 (culpability above a blood THC threshold); 2.5% of fatal crashes in France attributable to cannabis against 29% to alcohol; crash risk 2–3 times against 6–15 times for alcohol. Myocardial infarction: 4.8 times in the hour after use; mortality after infarction 2.5 to 4.2 times by frequency of use. Cancers: head and neck OR 2; lung OR 8.2. Burden: 0.2% of total disease burden in Australia. Editors' calculation from the suicide case–control percentages (16% against 2%): a crude odds ratio of about 9, which adjustment reduced to about 2.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable. Adjustment sets of the cited estimates are rarely given: 'a few confounding variables' for the Swedish 2.3; blood alcohol, age and time of crash for Laumon et al.; cigarettes, alcohol and other risk factors for Zhang et al.; cigarettes for the Tunisian lung-cancer estimate; social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence for the suicide case–control study.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The body reports several null or contrary findings (no excess respiratory cancer in the Kaiser Permanente cohort, three null head-and-neck case–control studies, no emphysema over 8 years, non-replication of impaired lung function, a null Australian psychosis-incidence trend, recovery after 28 days of abstinence), but the Summary and panels leave most of them out (see interpretation gap).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Second-hand, in the body: a 2.4-fold and, for ten or more uses by 18, a 2.3-fold risk of a schizophrenia diagnosis in Swedish conscripts and a dose–response over 27 years; pooled odds ratios of 1.4 (ever use) and 2.09 (the regular-use category) for psychotic symptoms or disorders, attenuated by adjustment, with no study assessing all major confounders and conflicting incidence trends; a lifetime risk of dependence of about 9% among people who use cannabis; crash risk raised 2–3 times (6–15 times for alcohol); subtle cognitive impairment in studies matched on pre-use ability, with recovery unclear; more bronchitis symptoms in people who smoke cannabis regularly, but long-term effects on lung function less clear and the one positive cohort finding not replicated; inconsistent cancer findings.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says epidemiological, clinical and laboratory studies "have established an association between cannabis use and adverse outcomes", and lists impaired respiratory function and cardiovascular disease among the most probable adverse effects (p. 1383). Panel 1 (p. 1388) lists impaired respiratory function in people who smoke regularly, psychotic symptoms and disorders in heavy use especially with a personal or family history of psychosis, and subtle cognitive impairment in daily use for 10 years or more; the Conclusions repeat the respiratory and family-history statements (p. 1389). Gaps: (1) the body calls long-term effects on lung function less clear and reports that the one positive cohort finding was not replicated (p. 1386), so impaired respiratory function is listed as probable without support in the review; (2) the body presents no evidence that a personal or family history modifies psychosis risk; (3) no duration threshold for cognitive impairment appears in the body, whose only 10-year figure describes the sample of one imaging study; (4) cardiovascular disease is in the Summary but in neither panel nor the Conclusions. On causation the Conclusions are measured: for the Panel 2 effects causality is not known, the size and reversibility of cognitive impairment remain unclear, and research should clarify the causative role of cannabis (p. 1389).

timeline.event: Swedish conscript cohort (Andréasson et al., 1987, as described here): 50 465 men followed for 15 years; those who had tried cannabis by 18 were 2.4 times more likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia.
US National Comorbidity Survey analysis cited for the lifetime dependence risks of other drugs (32% nicotine, 23% heroin, 17% cocaine, 15% alcohol, 11% stimulants).
WHO review of the health effects of cannabis (WHO Programme on Substance Abuse, 1997), the previous review this one updates.

Recovery after 28 days of abstinence (Pope et al., 2001), set against persistent dose-related impairment after 28 days (Bolla et al., 2002): the conflicting cognitive-recovery findings the review places side by side.

27-year follow-up of the Swedish cohort (Zammit et al., 2002): dose–response persisting after adjustment; 13% of schizophrenia cases estimated avertable. Supporting cohorts cited: the Netherlands (van Os et al., 2002), New Zealand (Arseneault et al., 2002; Fergusson et al., 2003) and Germany (Henquet et al., 2004).

Tests of the common-cause explanation of the link with other illicit drugs: a simulation showing shared risk factors could reproduce all the associations (Morral et al., 2002); a discordant-twin study in which the association persisted within pairs (Lynskey et al., 2003); fixed-effects regression that weakened but did not remove it (Fergusson et al., 2006).

Test of the incidence-trend prediction by the review's authors (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003): no clear rise in psychosis incidence in Australia despite steep rises in cannabis use. Also cited: a model judging it too early to see a rise in England and Wales (Hickman et al., 2007); rises in recent birth cohorts in south-east London (Boydell et al., 2006) and Zurich (Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2007); no rise in another British study (cited only via the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, 2008).
Systematic review of longitudinal general-population studies (Macleod et al., 2004), cited for doubts that statistical adjustment can remove confounding.

Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies: pooled OR 1.4 (ever use) and 2.09 (regular-use category) for psychotic outcomes, 1.49 for depression; suicide studies too heterogeneous to pool (as cited here).

Update by the first author (Hall, 2015): repeats much of this review's text and many of its figures, now calls the effect on respiratory function unclear, and adds the Dunedin IQ cohort and an absolute-risk estimate for psychosis; it does not cite this review.

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative review: cite it for its causal criteria and its 2009 reading of the evidence (as the authors'), and use it to find primary studies; take every number from the primary study (for dependence, the survey itself, card sc_anthony_1994; for the pooled psychosis and depression estimates, card sc_moore_2007). It overlaps heavily with the first author's 2015 update (card sc_hall_2015), so the two do not count as independent support. The causal question for psychosis was open in the review itself (common cause difficult to exclude; incidence trends conflicting); genetically informed tests are not discussed; later reviews of the psychosis evidence are appraised elsewhere in this round (Gage et al., 2016; Ksir & Hart, 2016; Gillespie & Kendler, 2021, whose title names genetically informed methods).

funding.funder: Beckley Foundation (WH); NHMRC Australia Fellowship (WH); National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales (LD); WHO, as part of a study of the contribution of illicit drug use to the global burden of disease (LD and WH). The authors state that the views are theirs alone and that no funding body influenced the decision to publish or had editorial control over the content (Acknowledgments, pp. 1389–1390).
funding.declared_conflicts: Conflicts of interest: "We declare that we have no conflicts of interest" (p. 1389).
funding.affiliations_note: School of Population Health, University of Queensland (WH); National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales (LD). The Acknowledgments describe the article as the updated version of a review first funded by the Australian Commonwealth Department of Health and Ageing in 1994 and updated in 2001 and 2003, linked to a report undertaken for the Beckley Foundation; Amanda Feilding is thanked for suggesting the update and commenting on the report, and Robin Room for contributions to that report. The paper does not describe the Beckley Foundation's aims. The authors' own work supplies the null Australian psychosis-incidence test and several framing statements. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For the review's open causal questions: for psychosis, comparisons that remove shared liability (co-twin and sibling designs, genetically informed methods with valid instruments) and incidence series with stable diagnostic coding as use and potency change; for cognition, prospective cohorts that test people before first use and again after sustained abstinence, against people who never used cannabis; for lung function, cohorts with enough people who smoke cannabis heavily but not tobacco.

domains.note: Databases, terms and a 10-year window are stated, but there are no inclusion criteria, record counts or selection procedure; key figures come from books outside the search, chiefly the authors' own; the authors chose the evidence.

No formal appraisal. General threats are discussed (other drug use, pre-existing differences, reverse causation, doubt about statistical adjustment) and specific limits are named for prenatal and cancer studies, but most estimates are given without their exposure definition, adjustment set or design quality.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Only 5 of 96 references are the authors' own, but one of them, their 2003 book, is the most-cited source (18 citations, editors' count) and carries the causal criteria, pattern-of-use and treatment-outcome figures; the null Australian incidence-trend test is the authors' own study. The main psychosis, driving and cancer evidence is by others.

Panel 2 and the Conclusions mark effects whose causal status is unknown; but the potency section states what higher THC content can do without data (only the authors' book is cited), and the panels add qualifiers the body does not support (family history, a 10-year threshold, impaired respiratory function).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm
domains.note: The body reports null and contrary findings and the case for confounding; the Summary and panels leave most of them out, so the evidence against harm is under-represented where readers look first. Benefits are outside the scope by design.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domain. The search is described but study selection is not explicit, and all figures are second-hand, many through the authors' own book. Cite the review for its causal criteria, its 2009 judgments (labelled as the authors') and as a pointer to the primary studies named in the key findings; take numbers from the primary studies. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft and must say its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Search as described: PubMed and Thomson Reuters Web of Science citation indexes (printed 'Thompson'), for articles published in the past 10 years on adverse health effects of cannabis, with a list of search terms (editors' count: 14), among them cannabis, marijuana smoking, adverse effects, lung diseases, traffic accidents, mental disorders and adolescent. Most selected studies were in English and published since 1997; more came from the papers selected and from books, edited works and reports. No inclusion criteria, record counts, screening or appraisal method are given.
key_findings.locator: Search strategy and selection criteria (box)

key_findings.finding: Causal criteria: the authors looked for an association in case–control and prospective studies; prospective evidence that use preceded the outcome, making reverse causation implausible; prospective studies controlling for confounders such as other drug use and characteristics on which people who use cannabis differ from others; and biological plausibility (criteria cited to Hall & Pacula, 2003, the first author's book). The focus was on effects with the greatest probability of affecting a substantial proportion of people who use cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Definitions and the main problem of interpretation: heavy or regular use is usually defined as daily or almost daily use, a pattern that predicts some adverse effects when continued over years (Hall & Pacula, 2003); with no data on THC dose, chronic use is usually defined as almost daily use over a period of years. Cannabis use is highly correlated with alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drug use, people who use regularly differ from others before they start, and some epidemiologists doubt that statistical adjustment succeeds (Macleod et al., 2004).
key_findings.locator: Pattern of cannabis use, 3rd paragraph (continued at the top of the right column, p. 1383); Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1386)

key_findings.finding: Pattern of use in the USA: about 10% of people who ever use cannabis go on to use it daily and 20–30% weekly (cited only to Hall & Pacula, 2003, the authors' book); use typically begins in the mid to late teens, peaks in the early to mid 20s and falls steeply with full-time work, marriage and children (Bachman et al., 1997).
key_findings.locator: Pattern of cannabis use, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The survey behind the 10% and 20–30% figures is not named; third-hand for claims. These are the review's only daily-use percentages: it gives no dependence figure for people who use daily (see key finding 8).

key_findings.finding: Potency: US THC content rose from under 2% in 1980 to 4.5% in 1997 and 8.5% in 2006 (ElSohly, 2008, a Potency Monitoring Project quarterly report, ref 13), and also rose in the Netherlands and probably elsewhere (McLaren et al., 2008); no data on changes in CBD content. THC content by product, as given: marijuana 0.5–5%, hashish 2–20%, hash oil 15–50% (UNODC World Drug Report 2006, ref 3).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Acute toxicity and acute adverse effects: the THC dose that kills rodents is very high, and the estimated fatal human dose (15 g to 70 g; Iversen, 2008; Gable, 2004) is much higher than a person who uses heavily smokes. The most common acute adverse effects are anxiety, panic reactions and psychotic symptoms, most often reported by people new to cannabis (Hall & Pacula, 2003).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Acute effects, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Driving, as cited: dose-related laboratory impairment of reaction time, information processing, perceptual–motor coordination, motor performance, attention and tracking (Ramaekers et al., 2004; Solowij, 1998); smaller on-road impairments than with intoxicating doses of alcohol because drivers slow down and take fewer risks (Smiley, 1999), but poorer responses to emergencies in some experiments (Robbe, 1994). Among 64 657 health-maintenance-organisation patients, those who used cannabis had more hospital admissions for injury than those who had stopped or never used, with motor-vehicle accident RR 1.96 after adjustment in men (Gerberich et al., 2003); a similar relation in 900 injured drivers and 900 age- and sex-matched controls (Mura et al., 2003; no estimate given); among 1420 Australian drivers killed, those with THC were more often culpable (OR 2.5), and those above a blood THC threshold printed as 5 μg/mL had a higher accident risk (OR 6.6) than those without THC (Drummer et al., 2004); among 6766 culpable and 3006 non-culpable French drivers (October 2001 to September 2003), OR 2.87 above a threshold printed as 1 μg/mL, a dose–response persisting after control for blood alcohol, age and time of crash, and 2.5% of fatal crashes attributable to cannabis against 29% to alcohol (Laumon et al., 2005). Driving after cannabis might increase crash risk 2–3 times, against 6–15 times with alcohol (Ramaekers et al., 2004).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Acute effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 1384, continued on p. 1385)
key_findings.note: The threshold units are probably misprinted (see reporting issues); take thresholds from the primary studies.

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy, as cited: high doses cause growth retardation and malformations in animals (Bloch, 1983); human evidence of birth defects is scarce and hard to interpret because women who use cannabis in pregnancy also use more tobacco, alcohol and other drugs, seek less antenatal care and have poorer nutrition; no increased risk of birth defects in a large group (Zuckerman et al., 1989). Reduced birthweight is the most consistent association (Fergusson et al., 2002); a meta-analysis found that regular cannabis smoking in pregnancy decreased birthweight, less than tobacco smoking, which the review attributes probably to carbon monoxide (English et al., 1997). Findings on child development are mixed (Fried & Smith, 2001; Tennes et al., 1985; Day et al., 1994, 655 women in Pittsburgh; Goldschmidt et al., 2000) and their causal reading is weakened by uncontrolled other drug use, parenting and genetic factors (Huizink & Mulder, 2006).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Reproductive effects, 1st–4th paragraphs (from p. 1385)

key_findings.finding: Dependence (impaired control over use and difficulty stopping despite harm) is the most common drug dependence after alcohol and tobacco in Australia, Canada and the USA, affecting 1–2% of adults in the past year and 4–8% in their lifetime (Hall & Pacula, 2003; Anthony, 2006). The lifetime risk of dependence among people who use cannabis is estimated at about 9%, rising to one in six among those who start in adolescence (both cited to Anthony, 2006, a book chapter); the equivalent lifetime risks are 32% for nicotine, 23% for heroin, 17% for cocaine, 15% for alcohol and 11% for stimulants (Anthony et al., 1994). Risk is highest with poor school achievement, deviant behaviour in childhood and adolescence, rebelliousness, poor parental relationships or parental drug and alcohol problems (Anthony, 2006).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 2nd paragraph (from the foot of the left column)
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The 9% and the comparison figures match the proportions of people who had ever used each drug who had ever met DSM-III-R dependence in the 1990–92 US National Comorbidity Survey, a cross-sectional survey (card sc_anthony_1994: cannabis 9.1%, tobacco 31.9%, heroin 23.1%, cocaine 16.7%, alcohol 15.4%, other stimulants 11.2%). The denominator is everyone who had ever used, not people who use regularly. The source of 'one in six' is not given beyond the chapter. The review contains no figure of 25–50% for dependence among people who use daily (text, panels and conclusions searched by the first and second readers), although Volkow et al. (2014) cite it for one (card sc_volkow_2014, reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Tolerance develops in animals and humans; the antagonist SR141716A precipitates a withdrawal syndrome in rats, mice and dogs (Lichtman & Martin, 2005); people seeking help to stop report anxiety, insomnia, appetite disturbance and depression (Budney & Hughes, 2006). Treatment-seeking rose over 20 years in the USA, Europe and Australia, including in the Netherlands, where cannabis use is decriminalised (Dutch national information system, 2004). Cognitive–behavioural therapy reduces use and problems, but only 15% of people remain abstinent 6–12 months after treatment (cited to Hall & Pacula, 2003).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 3rd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: The symptoms are listed without ranking; the ranking (most common) is in Hall (2015, p. 5).

key_findings.finding: Respiratory effects: long-term effects on respiratory function are called less clear (Tetrault et al., 2007); people who smoke cannabis regularly report more symptoms of chronic bronchitis (wheeze, sputum, chronic cough) than people who do not smoke (Tetrault et al., 2007); people who smoke only cannabis show impaired respiratory immune competence and more health-service use for respiratory infections (Tashkin et al., 2002). In a New Zealand cohort of 1037 young people followed to age 26, respiratory function was impaired in those dependent on cannabis (Taylor et al., 2002), but this was not replicated in longer US follow-up (Tashkin et al., 2002). Chronic cannabis smoking did not increase emphysema over 8 years in people who smoked only cannabis in the USA (Tashkin, 2005) and New Zealand (Aldington et al., 2007).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Cancer: cannabis smoke contains many of the carcinogens in tobacco smoke, some at higher concentrations (Moir et al., 2008), is mutagenic and carcinogenic in the mouse skin test, and chronic cannabis smoking goes with lung-cell changes that precede lung cancer in tobacco smokers (Tashkin, 1999). Epidemiology is inconsistent: no increased respiratory cancer in current or former cannabis smokers over 8.6 years among 64 855 Kaiser Permanente members (Sidney et al., 1997); head and neck squamous cell carcinoma OR 2 in 173 cases and 176 controls after adjustment for cigarettes, alcohol and other factors (Zhang et al., 1999), but three other case–control studies were null (Hashibe et al., 2005). Lung-cancer case–control studies are more consistent but confounded by cigarettes (Mehra et al., 2006): a Tunisian study of 110 hospital cases and 110 community controls, OR 8.2 after adjustment for cigarettes, and a pooled analysis of three Moroccan studies in which everyone who smoked cannabis also smoked tobacco (both cited to Berthiller et al., 2008); a dose–response with frequency of use in 79 cases under 55 and 324 community controls in New Zealand (Aldington et al., 2008); a US study whose associations were not significant after control for tobacco (Hashibe et al., 2006). The authors call for larger cohort and better case–control studies.
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 4th paragraph (end), 5th paragraph (continued on p. 1387) and 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular effects: cannabis and THC raise heart rate in a dose-dependent way, with quick tolerance in healthy young adults (Jones, 2002; Sidney, 2002). In a case-crossover study of 3882 people who had had a myocardial infarction, the risk of infarction was 4.8 times higher in the hour after cannabis use (Mittleman et al., 2001); in 1913 of them, mortality over 3.8 years showed a dose–response, 2.5 times for use less than weekly and 4.2 times for use more than weekly (Mukamal et al., 2008); laboratory studies show cannabis smoking provokes angina in people with heart disease (Gottschalk et al., 1977).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Chronic effects, 7th paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: Hall (2015, p. 10) describes the same case-crossover estimate as a quadrupling and its Table 1 as 3–4-fold; check Mittleman et al. (2001). The review gives no interval, number of people exposed or significance test for 4.8, 2.5 or 4.2.

key_findings.finding: Cognition, direction of effect: poor cognitive functioning is a risk factor for regular cannabis use, and whether chronic use impairs cognitive performance is not clear (Solowij, 1998). Studies that matched people who did and did not use cannabis on estimated pre-use intellectual function (Solowij, 1998) or on cognitive performance assessed before use (Block et al., 2002) found subtle cognitive impairments in people who used frequently and long term.
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › CNS effects, 1st paragraph (left column)
key_findings.note: Tests, exposure, comparison and abstinence are not given for these studies, and the second is cited to a paper whose title concerns cerebral blood flow (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cognitive deficits and recovery: deficits in verbal learning, memory and attention are most consistently reported in heavy use and have been related variously to duration and frequency of use and cumulative THC dose (Solowij et al., 2002); whether they reflect acute, residual or cumulative effects is debated. Whether function recovers after stopping is unclear: partial recovery after 2 years of abstinence, with event-related potentials still showing impaired information processing correlated with years of use (Solowij, 1998); 'indications of' persistent dose-related impairment after 28 days of abstinence in young people who used heavily for 5 years (Bolla et al., 2002); recovery after 28 days of abstinence (Pope et al., 2001).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › CNS effects, 2nd paragraph (left column, continued at the top of the right column)
key_findings.note: Hall (2015, p. 5) states the same two studies more firmly: persistent impairment (Bolla) and full recovery (Pope).

key_findings.finding: Brain imaging: after 26 hours of abstinence, people who used cannabis regularly had lower resting cerebral blood flow than controls in the posterior cerebellum and prefrontal cortex (Block et al., 2000); functional imaging showed less activity in memory and attention regions in people who used chronically than in people who did not, even after 28 days of abstinence (Quickfall & Crockford, 2006; Block et al., 2002); 15 people who had smoked five or more joints a day for 10 or more years had smaller hippocampal and amygdala volumes, the reductions increasing with duration of use (Yücel et al., 2008). The authors call for larger studies relating brain structure to cognitive impairment.
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › CNS effects, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Education: cannabis use is associated with poor educational attainment, but whether use causes poor school performance, follows from it or shares common causes is unclear (Lynskey & Hall, 2000, the first author's own review). Use before age 15 was related to early school leaving after adjustment for confounders in longitudinal studies (Ellickson et al., 1998). The most plausible explanation is called a combination of higher pre-existing risk, effects of regular use on cognition, affiliation with peers who reject school and a desire for an early transition to adulthood; adolescents who use cannabis and leave school early are more often unemployed and on welfare and less satisfied in their late 20s (Fergusson & Boden, 2008).
key_findings.locator: Health effects of cannabis › Psychosocial effects, 1st–2nd paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Other illicit drugs: in the USA, Australia and New Zealand people who used cannabis regularly were the most likely to go on to use heroin and cocaine, more so the earlier they started (Kandel, 2002). Three explanations are given (shared black market; common causes; pharmacological effects). A simulation showed that the common-cause hypothesis would reproduce all the associations (Morral et al., 2002); adjustment for confounders, including unmeasured fixed ones by fixed-effects regression (Fergusson et al., 2006), weakened but did not eliminate them (Hall & Lynskey, 2005, the first author's own review); in 136 monozygotic and 175 dizygotic twin pairs in which one twin had used cannabis before 17 and the other had not, the twin who used was more likely to use other illicit drugs, after control for non-shared environmental factors (Lynskey et al., 2003).
key_findings.locator: Other illicit drug use, 1st paragraph (p. 1387, continued on p. 1388) and 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Psychosis, Swedish conscripts: in a 15-year follow-up of 50 465 male conscripts, those who had tried cannabis by 18 were 2.4 times more likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia than those who had not; risk rose with frequency and stayed significant after adjustment for a few confounders; those who had used ten or more times by 18 were 2.3 times more likely (Andréasson et al., 1987). The 27-year follow-up showed a dose–response with frequency of use at 18 that persisted after adjustment, and estimated that 13% of schizophrenia cases could be averted if cannabis use were prevented (Zammit et al., 2002). Longitudinal studies in the Netherlands (van Os et al., 2002), Germany (Henquet et al., 2004) and New Zealand (Arseneault et al., 2002; Fergusson et al., 2003) are cited as supporting, all with associations persisting after adjustment.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 1st paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Exposure: self-reported use by 18 (tried; ten or more times); outcome: schizophrenia diagnosis; comparator: men who had not used; the adjustment set is not given here (Hall, 2015, p. 7, names personal psychiatric history by 18 and parental divorce for the 2.3). The 13% is an attributable fraction that assumes the association is causal.

key_findings.finding: Psychosis, pooled estimates: a meta-analysis of these longitudinal studies (Moore et al., 2007) reported a pooled OR of 1.4 (95% CI 1.20–1.65) for psychotic symptoms or psychotic disorders in people who had ever used cannabis, and OR 2.09 (1.54–2.84) in the category the review calls regular use, compared with no use. Reverse causation was addressed in most of the studies by excluding people with psychotic symptoms at baseline or adjusting for them. The common-cause hypothesis was "difficult to exclude", because the association was attenuated by adjustment and no study assessed all major confounders.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 2nd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: The outcome combines symptoms and disorders. The exposure categories, the studies pooled and their adjustment sets must be taken from Moore et al. (card sc_moore_2007). Hall (2015, p. 8) says reverse causation was addressed in some of these studies.

key_findings.finding: Incidence trends: evidence is called conflicting on whether schizophrenia incidence rose as cannabis use rose among young adults, as a causal account would predict. No clear increase in psychosis incidence in Australia despite steep rises in use in the 1980s and 1990s (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003, the authors' own study); too early to see an increase in England and Wales in the 1990s (Hickman et al., 2007, model projections); increases in recent birth cohorts in a British study (Boydell et al., 2006) and a Swiss study (Ajdacic-Gross et al., 2007); no increase in another British study (cited only to a 2008 Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs report).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Depression: associations are described as inconsistent and weak. A dose–response between frequency of use at 16 and depressive disorder was not significant after adjustment (Fergusson & Horwood, 1997); a meta-analysis gave OR 1.49 (95% CI 1.15–1.94), but its authors judged that confounding, and depressed young people being more likely to use cannabis, had not been excluded (Moore et al., 2007).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Suicide: in a New Zealand case–control study of serious suicide attempts requiring hospital admission, 16% of 302 people who attempted suicide met criteria for cannabis dependence or abuse, against 2% of 1028 community controls; adjustment for social disadvantage, depression and alcohol dependence substantially reduced but did not eliminate the association (OR 2) (Beautrais et al., 1999). Prospective evidence is mixed: a dose–response between frequency of use at 16 and self-reported suicide attempts did not persist after adjustment (Fergusson & Horwood, 1997); self-harm was associated with cannabis in women but not men after adjustment for depression and alcohol use (Patton et al., 1997); a meta-analysis found the studies too heterogeneous to estimate risk, few having excluded reverse causation or controlled confounding (Moore et al., 2007).
key_findings.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 5th–6th paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the rounded percentages: crude odds ratio about 9 ((0.16/0.84)/(0.02/0.98)), so adjustment reduced the estimate from about 9 to 2.

key_findings.finding: Potency and health: recent studies suggest potency may have increased in the late 1990s (McLaren et al., 2008); whether CBD content changed is unclear. The review then states, citing only the authors' book (Hall & Pacula, 2003), that the health effects of higher potency depend on whether people take in less THC when products are stronger and on their experience; that high THC content can increase anxiety, depression and psychotic symptoms in people new to cannabis and the risks of dependence and psychotic symptoms in people who use regularly, depending on how far they compensate for higher potency; and that it could raise the risk of road crashes. No study of potency and any health outcome is cited.
key_findings.locator: Increased THC content in cannabis products (single paragraph, left column)

key_findings.finding: Panel 1, acute adverse effects: anxiety and panic, especially in people new to cannabis; psychotic symptoms (at high doses); road crashes when driving while intoxicated. Chronic adverse effects: a dependence syndrome in around one in ten people who use cannabis; chronic bronchitis and impaired respiratory function in people who smoke regularly; psychotic symptoms and disorders in heavy use, especially with a history of psychotic symptoms or a family history of these disorders; impaired educational attainment in adolescents who use regularly; subtle cognitive impairment in daily use for 10 years or more. Panel 2, possible adverse effects of regular use with unknown causal relation: respiratory cancers; behavioural disorders in children whose mothers used cannabis in pregnancy; depressive disorders, mania and suicide; use of other illicit drugs by adolescents.
key_findings.locator: Panel 1; Panel 2
key_findings.note: Several Panel 1 statements go beyond the body; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: acute effects include anxiety and panic in people new to cannabis and a probable increased risk of crashes when driving intoxicated; use in pregnancy could reduce birthweight but does not seem to cause birth defects; whether it contributes to behavioural disorders in children is uncertain. Chronic use can produce dependence in 'as many as one in ten' people who use; people who use regularly have a higher risk of chronic bronchitis, impaired respiratory function and psychotic symptoms and disorders, most probably with a personal or family history of psychosis; impaired educational attainment is the most probable psychosocial effect; the explanation of the link with other illicit drugs remains contested; regular adolescent use might also affect young adults' mental health, the strongest evidence being for psychotic symptoms and disorders. For the Panel 2 effects causality is not known; for cognition the size and reversibility of impairment remain unclear; research should clarify the causal role of cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st–3rd paragraphs (from the foot of the left column)

key_findings.finding: Burden: the authors judge the public-health burden of cannabis probably modest compared with alcohol, tobacco and other illicit drugs. An Australian burden-of-disease study (Begg et al., 2007) estimated that cannabis caused 0.2% of total disease burden, 10% of the burden attributable to all illicit drugs, around 10% of the burden attributed to alcohol (2.3%) and 2.5% of that attributable to tobacco (7.8%).
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 0.2/2.3 = 8.7% and 0.2/7.8 = 2.6%, consistent with the rounded figures. The burden estimate treats the cannabis effects it counts as causal.

reporting_issues.issue: Blood THC thresholds are printed in μg/mL: higher crash risk above 5 μg/mL (Drummer et al., 2004) and more culpability above 1 μg/mL (Laumon et al., 2005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a misprint for ng/mL, a thousandfold difference; take any threshold from the primary studies, not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Pittsburgh cohort (Day et al., ref 33) is described as children born to 655 women between 1990 and 1995 and tested at age 3, but the cited paper is dated 1994 (Neurotoxicol Teratol 1994; 16: 169–75).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dates cannot be right as printed (a 1994 paper cannot report 3-year outcomes of births up to 1995); the same dates recur in Hall (2015, p. 4). Take the cohort's dates from the primary.

reporting_issues.issue: The Tunisian lung-cancer case–control study (110 cases, 110 controls, OR 8.2) and the pooled analysis of three Moroccan studies are both cited to ref 53, whose title describes a pooled analysis of three studies in the Maghreb (Berthiller et al., 2008).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two sentences may describe one source rather than two independent findings; whether the Tunisian estimate is part of the pooled analysis must be checked in the primary. In Hall (2015, p. 10) the Tunisian sentence has no citation.

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary lists impaired respiratory function among the most probable adverse effects, and Panel 1 and the Conclusions list it as a chronic effect of regular smoking, while the body says long-term effects on respiratory function are less clear and that the one positive cohort finding (Taylor et al., 2002) was not replicated in longer US follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary statement is at most weakly supported by the evidence the review presents (one unreplicated cohort finding and impaired respiratory immune competence); the 2015 update calls the effect on respiratory function unclear (Hall, 2015, p. 12). Do not cite the Summary or Panel 1 for impaired lung function.

reporting_issues.issue: Panel 1 and the Conclusions say psychotic symptoms and disorders occur most probably in people with a personal or family history of psychosis, but the psychosis section presents no evidence on modification of risk by personal or family history.
reporting_issues.consequence: The qualifier is an assertion in this review; a claim on it needs primary evidence (Henquet et al., 2004, whose title names predisposition for psychosis, is cited only as a supporting cohort).

reporting_issues.issue: Panel 1 limits subtle cognitive impairment to daily use for 10 years or more and lists acute psychotic symptoms as occurring at high doses; the 10-year threshold has no basis in the body beyond the sample of one imaging study (Yücel et al., 2008). The dose qualifier appears in the body only in the potency paragraph (p. 1389), which states, citing no study beyond the authors' book, that high THC content can increase psychotic symptoms in people new to cannabis; the acute-effects text links psychotic symptoms to inexperience, not to dose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The duration threshold and the dose qualifier cannot be traced to evidence in the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Cardiovascular disease is among the most probable adverse effects in the Summary, and the body says evidence supports adverse cardiovascular effects, but neither panel nor the Conclusions mention it; Panel 2 lists mania, which the body does not discuss.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary devices disagree with each other and with the body; cite the body for cardiovascular effects. The review offers no evidence on mania.

reporting_issues.issue: The dependence figure changes denominator: the body gives a lifetime risk of about 9% among people who use cannabis (p. 1386); Panel 1 lists dependence in around one in ten people who use as a chronic adverse effect (p. 1388); the Conclusions attach it to chronic use ('as many as one in ten', p. 1389).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is a lifetime proportion among everyone who had ever used (card sc_anthony_1994), not a risk among people who use regularly or chronically; claims must carry the ever-use denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The British study that found no increase in schizophrenia incidence is cited only to a 2008 report of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ref 92), not to the study itself.
reporting_issues.consequence: The null incidence finding is third-hand and its primary is unnamed; it cannot be appraised from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The studies said to have matched people who did and did not use cannabis on pre-use ability are cited to a book (Solowij, 1998) and to a paper whose title concerns memory-related cerebral blood flow (Block et al., 2002); no test, sample or effect size is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subtle-cognitive-impairment conclusion cannot be traced to a primary cognitive study from this review; check the primaries before citing it.
